name: Daria Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew building and repairing power lines for the electricity company. I have a two-year technical diploma, but I still teach an apprentice to read the pole label and test the wire before listening to an office instruction. A good repair is quiet when we leave, and I like that. My husband Elias and I have grown children, more than a year of expenses saved, and I had thought of working until about sixty-six if my health holds. This job pays well and there are plenty of other line crews nearby. I have never used AI and do not intend to trust a new tool without seeing it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew to keep the same tests and let the office shorten its reports. A screen can save a clerk time; it cannot make a line safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shifts and pay would continue, and Elias and I have a substantial reserve. I would rather keep earning toward our planned retirement than learn a software trick that saves a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs with the usual meter and isolation checks. During the first year I would mark any new report that leaves the test reading out before I sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The tools in my truck and the household account would look much the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which reading must be on the report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The voltage after isolation, with the switch number beside it. If I cannot find those two facts quickly, I send the form back before the next crew sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let an apprentice use AI for the form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice can learn a tool, but the apprentice must explain the physical reading first. I would not have a phone answer for the person holding the meter.

say: **Physical tests** still decide whether a line is safe.
**Shorter reports** are acceptable when isolation readings remain clear.
think: My **pay and shifts** stay secure under a plateau.
Our **strong reserve** supports the retirement plan we already had.
do: **Keep** leading repairs with meter and isolation checks.
**Return** any new form missing the voltage and switch number.
S0.quote: A screen can save a clerk time; it cannot make a line safe.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and makes the apprentice explain a real reading first.
Her **higher pay and savings** make this mild change financially unthreatening.

steps.text: Keep leading line repairs with usual meter checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say software can speed booking and buying, but it should not decide a repair time from a car map. I would keep the crew’s own route notes beside any new schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may change quickly, yet I expect my crew and wage to continue for now. If a rushed plan makes repairs longer, the younger workers might have to carry the strain; I can speak up without needing to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would collect six examples of truck access and isolation time and take them to the depot supervisor. In the first year I would keep the crew rota while asking for a field trial before the new target becomes fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a planner missing the ground conditions. I am secure enough not to make a job decision from one bad route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one example show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The road to the north feeder has a bend the bucket truck cannot make. The car map looks shorter, but the bucket truck would have to drive around the block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask a union to handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the six sheets to the supervisor first. If the supervisor refuses a field test, I would ask other crew leads to raise the access problem together.

say: **Booking and buying** change first, before capable field robots can do physical power-line repairs.
**Car maps** cannot set safe truck repair times alone.
think: My **lineworker wage** looks secure in this slower disruption because our crew still handles the physical repairs.
Younger **crew members** might bear the pressure of rushed targets.
do: **Collect** six actual bucket-truck access and line isolation examples before the supervisor changes repair targets.
**Request** a field trial before repair targets are fixed.
feel: **Uneasy** about poor ground detail, secure about income.
S1.quote: The car map looks shorter, but the bucket truck would have to drive around the block.
fieldNote: She expects **income security** and starts with a supervisor rather than a job search.
Her **group request** is conditional on a refused field test, so no collective action is tagged yet.

steps.text: Keep crew rota while collecting six repair access examples
Wait for a field trial before accepting new repair targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices thinking AI can take planning by 2028, while capable line repair robots come about 2031. Three years of physical work remain between those dates, and the crew should use them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had thought of working until about sixty-six, so robots arriving when I am near sixty-three might cut my high-pay years. We have over a year of expenses saved and many local utilities. A cash cushion is not the same as lifetime income for a lineworker leaving work at sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get a detailed retirement budget with Elias and compare it with an early stop at about sixty-three. If field robots cut my repair shifts after 2031 and the full budget supports it, I would retire three years ahead of my plan; if the numbers fail, I would apply for a posted local line-safety job with pay that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the choice of when to stop, not overwhelmed. The family account gives us room to work through the options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count in the early retirement budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Regular food and housing bills, home repairs and the income we can rely on after work. I would not multiply one good year of callouts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the grown children to bridge a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Elias and I would use our own savings and work options before asking our children to give up their plans.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches planning before capable field robots arrive around 2031.
**Apprentices** still have physical linework during the gap.
think: Robots could cut **high-pay years** before my intended age of sixty-six.
A **one-year reserve** cannot alone guarantee lifetime retirement income.
do: **Compare** a sixty-three retirement budget with our usual bills.
**Retire** three years early if post-2031 shifts fall and full costs are covered.
**Apply** for a posted local line-safety job if early retirement fails and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about losing control of retirement timing.
S2.quote: A cash cushion is not the same as lifetime income for a lineworker leaving work at sixty-three.
fieldNote: She describes an **actual earlier exit** relative to her own age-sixty-six plan, conditional on affordability.
If retirement fails, her **job application** needs a posted role and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Retire three years early if post-2031 shifts fall and lifetime costs are covered
Apply for posted local line-safety work if early retirement fails and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives the utility time to show a robot on an old, wet line before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Full field robots follow around 2034; a training film would not settle whether a crew can stop one safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be around sixty-six when the physical robots arrive, which is near the age I have in mind for retirement. That could fit our plan, but I would not leave until Elias and I confirm the figures and decide we want to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and review our retirement plan with Elias every year. In the first year after 2031, if I am still working, I would watch a field robot trial; if the employer requires controls for my current work and pays for hands-on instruction, I would take that instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful, with less personal income risk than the fast picture. I can wait for a real trial instead of guessing at a machine from a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the field trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker must be able to stop the robot at a bad isolation reading, and the reason should stay in the log. I would not accept a repair robot reset button controlled from an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-six even if the job remains?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, if the budget and our wishes line up. The robot arrival would not be the reason for moving the date forward.

say: **Old wet lines** should be part of robot trials before 2034.
**Worker stop controls** matter more than a training film.
think: Field robots around **sixty-six** may meet my planned retirement period.
I still need **budget figures** and a personal decision before leaving.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and review retirement finances yearly.
**Watch** a field robot trial after 2031 if still employed.
**Take** paid hands-on robot controls instruction if required for current work.
feel: **Watchful**, with limited immediate household income risk.
S3.quote: I would not accept a repair robot reset button controlled from an office.
fieldNote: She links **retirement** to her own plan, not a promised pension age.
Her **controls instruction** requires ongoing employment, employer payment and a need in current work.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review retirement finances yearly
Watch field robot trial after 2031 if still employed
Take employer-paid robot controls instruction if required for current work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable field robots around 2039. I expect to have finished paid linework before the machines can do full repairs, provided our retirement plan still adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be near sixty-eight at the first date and around seventy-one at the second. The card gives me enough time to keep earning and check the family plan, and a younger crew will face the robot repair questions directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs while I am working and review retirement costs with Elias each year. In the first year after 2036, if I am still employed, I would show an apprentice how to verify a robot work order against the pole label and meter; if retired, I would leave the work to the active crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our living if the retirement budget holds. I still want the apprentice to know the wire is real when the work order comes from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake would you teach the apprentice to catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give the apprentice a sample order with the wrong switch number and ask for the actual pole label. A printed robot work order is no excuse for skipping a physical power-line check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 2039 robot date make you retire sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Elias and I would follow our own affordable date, not move it forward for a machine expected after that.

say: **2036 thinking AI** arrives before capable field robots around 2039.
**Pole labels and meters** remain essential for apprentices.
think: The **long runway** gives time to earn and confirm retirement costs.
I expect to finish **paid linework** before full repair robots if finances allow.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and review retirement costs with Elias yearly.
**Teach** robot work-order checks after 2036 only if still employed.
feel: **Calm** about living if our retirement budget holds.
S4.quote: A printed robot work order is no excuse for skipping a physical power-line check.
fieldNote: She expects **retirement before robots** only if the complete household budget figures continue to work.
She favors **apprenticeship teaching** without treating individual instruction as group action.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and review retirement costs with Elias yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots around 2031 could shorten my high-pay years before Elias and I intended to stop work. A written account of our retirement costs and a posted local job at enough pay would help us choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a veteran lineworker owes a new apprentice. I owe the line apprentice a meter in hand, not a neat story about a robot being safe.

portrait: **Daria Ibrahim**, 58, leads power line repairs and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She and husband Elias have **grown children**, high lineworker pay, over a year saved and many nearby utility employers.
She has **never used AI**, prizes apprenticeship checks and is slow to accept tools without a wet-line trial.
In **AGI by 2028**, she considers retirement three years earlier only if the full household budget is affordable.
The **2031 and 2036 pictures** give her time to work toward her intended retirement period while teaching physical checks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her high-pay repair shifts around 2031, before her intended retirement age.
whatWouldHelp: A written **retirement budget** would show whether stopping three years early is affordable.
A posted **local safety job** at bill-covering pay would protect income if the budget fails.
headlineQuote: I owe the line apprentice a meter in hand, not a neat story about a robot being safe.
